intro: In 622, according to Muslim tradition, Muhammad and his followers left Mecca for the town that became Medina. The surahs Muslims date after that move sound different from the earlier ones. They are longer. They speak to a community with a mosque, neighbors, allies and enemies. They give rules: how to fast, how to divide an estate, how to write a contract, when fighting is allowed and when it must stop. This unit reads four of those surahs closely: Al-Baqarah, the longest in the book, and An-Nisa, Al-Ma'idah and Al-Hujurat.

These surahs hold the verses people quote most, for and against Islam: the Throne Verse, no compulsion in religion, stand firm for justice even against yourselves, killing one person is like killing all people, to each a law and a way, nations and tribes that you may know one another. They also hold verses on wives, on Jews and Christians, and on war that readers have argued over for fourteen centuries. You will read each one with the verses around it, with the occasion Muslim commentators attached to it, and with the ways classical and modern readers have understood it.

By the end you will be able to find your way around a long surah, explain what a Medinan verse says and to whom, and set two readings of the same verse side by side without deciding which is true. That last skill is the one a public-school study of scripture asks for. It is also the one that commentators like al-Tabari practiced when they recorded every reading they knew and let the reader weigh them.
bigQuestion: How do the Medinan surahs build a community, and how have readers across fourteen centuries understood their verses on law, justice and other faiths?

timeline.t: Muhammad and his followers move from Mecca to Medina (the hijra); Medinan surahs begin
The qibla turns from Jerusalem to Mecca (2:142–150); Battle of Badr
Fasting in Ramadan is set out (2:183–187), by tradition
Battle of Uhud; verses of An-Nisa on orphans, widows and inheritance
Treaty of Hudaybiyyah between Medina and Mecca
Conquest of Mecca; year of delegations; Al-Hujurat, by tradition
Farewell pilgrimage; verses of Al-Ma'idah, by tradition; death of Muhammad
Al-Tabari's commentary records many readings of 2:256 and other verses
Ibn Kathir's commentary; he writes that no one is forced into Islam
World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago; Alexander Russell Webb speaks for Islam
Pickthall publishes The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, this course's text

words.d: a surah that Muslim tradition dates after the move to Medina in 622
the direction Muslims face in prayer; changed from Jerusalem to Mecca in about 624
the Throne Verse, 2:255; the most recited single verse in Muslim practice
compulsion; 2:256 says there is none in religion
naskh; the classical theory that a later verse can set aside an earlier ruling
a report about the event a verse answered (asbab al-nuzul)
usury or interest on loans, forbidden in 2:275
the fixed shares of inheritance set in 4:11–12
fair dealing, justice; the word in 4:135 and 5:8
Ahl al-Kitab; Jews and Christians, and others with a scripture
mindfulness of God; the measure of nobility in 49:13
the traditional biography of Muhammad, written down in the eighth and ninth centuries

test.q: Which surah is the longest in the Qur'an?
test.why: Al-Baqarah, Surah 2, has 286 ayahs, more than any other surah.

test.q: What marks a surah as Medinan?
choices: It was found in Medina's mosque
It has fewer than twenty verses
It is dated by tradition after the hijra of 622
test.why: Muslim scholars sort surahs by whether tradition places them before or after the move to Medina.

test.q: In Al-Baqarah's story of Adam, what did God teach Adam?
test.why: 2:31 says God taught Adam the names, which the angels could not give.

test.q: What does 2:62 say about Jews, Christians and Sabians?
choices: Those who believe in God and the last day and do right have their reward
They may not eat with Muslims
test.why: 2:62, like 5:69, promises reward to those of these groups who believe and do right; readers differ on its scope.
These verses prescribe fasting, name Ramadan, and set the hours from dawn to night.

test.q: What is the Throne Verse mostly about?
test.why: 2:255 opens with tawhid and describes God as never sleeping, all-knowing, whose throne spans heaven and earth.

test.q: Which verse says there is no compulsion in religion?
test.why: 2:256, right after the Throne Verse, begins There is no compulsion in religion.

test.q: Why did some early scholars say 2:256 was abrogated, and what did most say?
choices: Some tied it to later fighting verses; most read it as standing
Most said it was about fasting
test.why: A minority held later verses set it aside; most, including Ibn Kathir, read it as a rule against forcing faith.

choices: Not to burden the community beyond its strength
test.why: The closing prayer of Al-Baqarah asks not to be tasked beyond capacity and for forgiveness.

test.q: What change did 4:11–12 make, according to historians and many Muslim scholars?
choices: They gave everything to the eldest son
They gave women fixed shares where before they often had none
test.why: The inheritance verses assign fixed shares to daughters, wives and mothers.

test.q: How have modern Muslim scholars handled 4:34?
choices: They read it in several ways: as bounded by hadith, as tied to its era, or with the verb read as to separate
They all agree it must be read literally
They say it is about inheritance
test.why: Modern readers, including women scholars, have offered several readings; the disagreement is part of the tradition.

test.q: Which rabbinic text has a close parallel to 5:32?
test.why: Sanhedrin 4:5 says one who destroys a single life is as if he destroyed a whole world.

test.q: How do most commentators, classical and modern, explain 5:51 on not taking Jews and Christians as awliya?
choices: As a ban on all contact
As about wartime alliances in Medina
test.why: From al-Tabari on, many tie 5:51 to protective pacts with tribes at war with the community.

test.q: What does 5:48 tell the different communities to do?
choices: Vie with one another in good works
test.why: Pickthall: So vie one with another in good works; God will explain the differences on the last day.

test.q: What purpose does 49:13 give for nations and tribes?
choices: That they may know one another
That they may rule one another
test.why: 49:13 says people were made nations and tribes that they may know one another, and that the noblest is the best in conduct.

write.prompt: Does the Qur'an, in its Medinan surahs, tell Muslims to keep apart from people of other faiths or to live among them? Cite 2:256, 5:48 and 49:13, and at least one harder verse such as 5:51. Explain what each says, what occasion commentators attach to it, and how a classical reader and a modern reader have understood it.
tips: Name each verse as surah:ayah and the surah's name, and say which translation you used.
Attribute every reading: al-Tabari records, Ibn Kathir holds, modern scholars argue.
Give the occasion of a verse before you say what it means today.
Compare readings; do not decide which faith or reading is true.
Use the unit's terms: Medinan, occasion of revelation, abrogation, People of the Book, taqwa.
